item.title: Edition #47: Washington Sides With OpenAI in the New York Times Copyright Fight; OpenAI Says Its Next Model Is Good Enough at Hacking to Need Extra Guardrails; Anthropic Ships Cheaper Claude Models That Say No Less Often
item.description: Washington backs OpenAI in the New York Times copyright case; OpenAI says its next model crosses its own critical threshold for hacking ability; Anthropic ships cheaper, less restrictive Claude models; Dell books a record $60.9 billion in AI orders; Wonderful doubles to a $5 billion valuation; McKinsey finds a third of companies skipping software purchases because AI can build it; and HiddenLayer raises $100 million to secure enterprise AI.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Washington Sides With OpenAI in the New York Times Copyright Fight

The federal government filed a brief supporting OpenAI in the New York Times' lawsuit over training AI systems on copyrighted articles and books without permission, arguing that restricting AI training would hurt American competitiveness and scientific progress. It is not a ruling, and the government is not the one deciding the case. But it is an unusually direct intervention in a dispute that could set the rules for how every AI company sources its training material.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. OpenAI Says Its Next Model Is Good Enough at Hacking to Need Extra Guardrails

OpenAI disclosed that its forthcoming Astra model is the first to cross the "critical" cybersecurity line in its own risk framework, meaning it can find and exploit software flaws on its own without a human directing it. The company plans to release the model soon while restricting access to its most advanced offensive capabilities and adding new abuse monitoring. Outside researchers have not been able to verify the claims independently.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. Anthropic Ships Cheaper Claude Models That Say No Less Often

Anthropic released updated versions of its most capable models, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, with better performance, lower prices, and fewer cases where safety filters block harmless requests. Fable is available to everyone; Mythos stays limited to vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences partners. The company also added an option for business customers to run the models without their data leaving their own systems.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Dell Books a Record $60.9 Billion in AI Orders in a Single Quarter

Dell reported $47 billion in quarterly revenue, up 58 percent, on the back of a record $60.9 billion in new AI server orders and a backlog that now sits at $95 billion. Its AI customer count jumped from 5,000 to 6,500 in three months, and the company raised full-year guidance by $25 billion. The numbers are one of the clearest signals yet that the money being spent on AI infrastructure is still accelerating, not leveling off.

Source: Dell Technologies · Read more →

5. Wonderful Doubles Its Valuation to $5 Billion in Under Six Months

The Israeli-Dutch startup raised $550 million led by Insight Partners, more than doubling the valuation it set in March. Founded in early 2025, Wonderful began with AI customer service agents built for non-English-speaking markets and has since expanded into a broader platform for wiring AI tools into company systems. Salesforce joined as a first-time investor.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. A Third of Companies Skipped a Software Purchase Because AI Could Build It

McKinsey's annual global AI survey found that nearly a third of organizations decided against buying at least one software product or feature because they could now build it in-house with AI coding tools. The share of large companies scaling AI agents in at least one business function climbed from 27 to 40 percent. The catch: 80 percent report individual productivity gains, but only 37 percent can point to actual financial impact.

Source: McKinsey · Read more →

7. HiddenLayer Raises $100 Million as Companies Scramble to Secure Their AI

The Austin startup, which builds tools to protect AI models and agents from tampering and attack, closed a $100 million round led by Delta-v Capital with Morgan Stanley, Microsoft's venture arm, and Booz Allen Hamilton participating. HiddenLayer says revenue grew more than tenfold over the past year. Analysts expect businesses to spend roughly $2.8 billion on AI security this year, up 83 percent from 2025.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #46: The Pentagon Hands ChatGPT and Grok to Three Million Military and Civilian Workers; Brussels Decides ChatGPT Is a Search Engine, and Puts It Under Europe's Strictest Rules; Anthropic Commits $35 Billion to a Single Texas Data Center
item.description: Edition #46 — Wednesday, September 2, 2026. The Pentagon switched on ChatGPT Mil and Grok for Government for three million defense workers. The European Commission designated ChatGPT a Very Large Online Search Engine under the Digital Services Act. Anthropic committed $35 billion to a Lambda-run Texas data center in which Nvidia plays three roles. Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell sued Anthropic and named its founders personally. Runway unveiled Solaris, an interface world model that generates working software frame by frame. Clay lined up a round at a $7 billion valuation. And McKinsey found a third of companies have skipped a software purchase because AI could build it instead.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. The Pentagon Hands ChatGPT and Grok to Three Million Military and Civilian Workers

The Defense Department switched on two new assistants — OpenAI's ChatGPT Mil and xAI's Grok for Government — inside GenAI.mil, the internal platform that already carried Google's Gemini. Roughly three million service members, civilian employees and contractors can now use them for unclassified desk work: planning, policy, logistics and the mountain of paperwork that comes with all three. Officials framed running rival models side by side as a hedge against getting locked into any single vendor.

Source: Fortune · Read more →

2. Brussels Decides ChatGPT Is a Search Engine, and Puts It Under Europe's Strictest Rules

The European Commission designated ChatGPT a “Very Large Online Search Engine” under the Digital Services Act, alongside new platform designations for Reddit and Roblox. The trigger was scale: OpenAI reported about 159 million average monthly users of ChatGPT search in the EU, more than triple the 45 million threshold. OpenAI has four months to comply with obligations on risk assessment, transparency and researcher access, and fines can reach 6% of global revenue.

Source: European Commission · Read more →

3. Anthropic Commits $35 Billion to a Single Texas Data Center — and Nvidia Sits on Three Sides of the Deal

Anthropic signed a $35 billion agreement to rent computing capacity from Lambda at a roughly 350-megawatt site in Nueces County, Texas, built by former crypto miner Hut 8. Nvidia is the chip supplier, an equity backer of Lambda, and the anchor tenant on the wider campus, an arrangement critics have started calling circular financing. It lands days after Anthropic committed $45 billion to a separate West Virginia campus, putting the company's recent cloud bookings near $80 billion.

Source: TechRepublic · Read more →

4. Sony and Warner Sue Anthropic Over Tens of Thousands of Songs — and Name Its Founders Personally

Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell filed suit in California federal court, accusing Anthropic of a “brazen campaign” of torrenting and scraping copyrighted compositions to train Claude, with songs from “Hallelujah” to “Uptown Funk” named in the complaint. Unusually, the filing names CEO Dario Amodei and co-founder Benjamin Mann as individual defendants. The publishers want a jury trial and up to $150,000 per infringed work, which means all three major music publishers are now litigating against the same company.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. Runway's Solaris Skips the Code and Draws Working Software One Frame at a Time

Runway unveiled Solaris, which it calls the first “interface world model” — a system that generates an app's screen live as you click, drag or speak to it, rather than writing code that a browser then renders. Everything you see is the model's output, painted frame by frame at 720p. It is not a public product yet; Runway says it is working with early partners, and the obvious question is whether software imagined on the fly can ever be reliable enough to trust.

Source: Runway · Read more →

6. Clay Lines Up a Round at a $7 Billion Valuation, Its Fourth Markup in Eighteen Months

The New York sales-automation startup agreed to new funding led by Wellington Management at a $7 billion pre-money valuation, according to Axios. Clay was worth $3.1 billion a year ago and $5 billion in January, a climb that says as much about investor appetite as about the company. The round size has not been disclosed, and it is not clear the deal has formally closed.

Source: Axios · Read more →

7. A Third of Companies Have Skipped Buying Software Because AI Could Build It Instead

McKinsey's annual State of AI survey found 32% of organizations passed on at least one software purchase because coding assistants made building it in-house look cheaper. Among the small group seeing real profit from AI, that figure approaches half. The catch buried in the same report: the share of companies reporting an actual earnings boost from AI has stayed flat, and one in five now says running costs are limiting how much they use it.

Source: McKinsey · Read more →

item.title: Edition #45: DeepSeek Nears a $7.4 Billion Raise at a $74 Billion Valuation, With a Shanghai IPO in Sight; NPR Tested Six Chatbots Against Foreign Propaganda. They Did Better Than Expected; California's Legislature Adjourns Today With Two Dozen AI Bills Still Unfinished
item.description: Edition #45 — Monday, August 31, 2026. DeepSeek Nears a $7.4 Billion Raise at a $74 Billion Valuation, With a Shanghai IPO in Sight. NPR Tested Six Chatbots Against Foreign Propaganda. They Did Better Than Expected. California's Legislature Adjourns Today With Two Dozen AI Bills Still Unfinished. Australia Signs Off on Mandatory Power and Water Rules for Big AI Data Centres. The FTC Finalizes Penalties Over an AI Ad Service That Claimed to Listen Through Your Phone. Stability AI Raises $76 Million From the Record Labels That Once Saw It as a Threat. AI Is Quietly Raising the Bar for Entry-Level Jobs, a Survey of 1,000 Hiring Managers Finds.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. DeepSeek Nears a $7.4 Billion Raise at a $74 Billion Valuation, With a Shanghai IPO in Sight

The Chinese lab that stunned the industry last year by building competitive AI models on a shoestring is now raising roughly $7.4 billion at a $74 billion pre-money valuation, according to the Wall Street Journal and South China Morning Post. DeepSeek is reportedly adding about a gigawatt of computing capacity and could file to list on Shanghai's STAR Market as soon as the end of this year. The irony is hard to miss: the company that proved AI could be built cheaply now needs billions to keep competing.

Source: Tech Startups · Read more →

2. NPR Tested Six Chatbots Against Foreign Propaganda. They Did Better Than Expected

NPR and the ratings firm NewsGuard built 30 questions around false narratives pushed by China, Iran and Russia, then put them to ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Meta AI, Grok and Claude, alongside four search engines. The chatbots correctly flagged the falsehoods about three-quarters of the time, outperforming the search engines. Researchers noted the phrasing mattered: asking “did this happen?” got better answers than assuming it had.

Source: NPR · Read more →

3. California's Legislature Adjourns Today With Two Dozen AI Bills Still Unfinished

Lawmakers in Sacramento worked through the weekend ahead of tonight's deadline, with around 30 AI-related bills in play covering chatbot safety for kids, algorithmic management of workers, healthcare disclosure and copyright protection for creative work. Only a handful have cleared both chambers so far. Anything that passes lands on Governor Newsom's desk, and he has until September 30 to sign or veto.

Source: Transparency Coalition · Read more →

4. Australia Signs Off on Mandatory Power and Water Rules for Big AI Data Centres

All nine of Australia's governments agreed to a single national rulebook for large data centres, with obligations to underwrite their own new power supply, cover their full grid connection costs so household bills are not affected, dial back consumption when the grid is strained, and meet water efficiency standards. Canberra also stood up a new Office of AI to coordinate policy. The standards are expected to be legislated early next year.

Source: Clayton Utz · Read more →

5. The FTC Finalizes Penalties Over an AI Ad Service That Claimed to Listen Through Your Phone

Cox Media Group and two partner firms marketed an “Active Listening” product they said used AI to overhear conversations picked up by smart devices and target ads accordingly. Regulators found it did nothing of the sort. The companies were actually reselling email lists bought from data brokers at a markup, and now owe $930,000 and face 20 years of FTC oversight.

Source: Federal Trade Commission · Read more →

6. Stability AI Raises $76 Million From the Record Labels That Once Saw It as a Threat

The company behind Stable Diffusion closed a $76 million Series B backed in part by Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music and the game publisher Electronic Arts. It is a notable turn for a firm that spent years fighting copyright suits from rights holders. The money suggests entertainment giants would rather help shape generative AI tools than litigate them out of existence.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

7. AI Is Quietly Raising the Bar for Entry-Level Jobs, a Survey of 1,000 Hiring Managers Finds

ZipRecruiter's annual employer report, based on a June survey of more than 1,000 recruiters and hiring managers, found 92% now use AI in some form. More telling: 38% have moved basic data work off junior staff and onto software, and 31% have raised the experience they require for entry-level roles as a result. The rungs on the career ladder are not disappearing so much as moving further apart.

Source: ZipRecruiter Economic Research · Read more →

item.title: Edition #44: Nvidia Agrees to Buy Hugging Face, the Internet's Library of Open AI Models, for $12.9 Billion; Federal Judge Rules the Pentagon Illegally Blacklisted Anthropic; Anthropic Paper Shows AI Systems Fixing Their Own Safety Problems, Faster and Cheaper Than People
item.description: Nvidia agrees to buy Hugging Face for $12.9 billion; a federal judge rules the Pentagon illegally blacklisted Anthropic; a new Anthropic paper shows AI systems repairing their own safety training more cheaply than human researchers; a16z raises $1.1 billion for AI hardware; Lambda borrows another $1 billion for Nvidia chips; Georgia clears a 3.2-gigawatt power deal for OpenAI's largest data center without a public vote; and Meta shuts the loophole that let its smart glasses record with the warning light covered.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Nvidia Agrees to Buy Hugging Face, the Internet's Library of Open AI Models, for $12.9 Billion

Nvidia has agreed to acquire Hugging Face, the site where developers around the world share and download free AI models, according to The Information. The chipmaker turned down a chance to buy in at $7 billion last year; the price is now nearly double that. Owning the largest hub for open models helps Nvidia keep customers from drifting to the in-house chips that OpenAI, Google, Amazon and Anthropic are all now building.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. Federal Judge Rules the Pentagon Illegally Blacklisted Anthropic

A California judge found that labeling Anthropic a national security supply-chain risk was unlawful retaliation for the company's public criticism of the government, calling the move arbitrary and a violation of the First and Fifth Amendments. The designation had barred every federal agency from working with the Claude maker. A second Anthropic suit against the Defense Department is still moving through court in Washington.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. Anthropic Paper Shows AI Systems Fixing Their Own Safety Problems, Faster and Cheaper Than People

A new Anthropic paper describes automated researchers that read the literature, propose a fix, and retrain a model, then keep whatever works. Across ten tests for misbehavior, the system improved every score without making the model worse elsewhere. The paper puts the cost at roughly $4 an hour versus $150 for a human researcher, and says the machine's best ideas beat the humans' within six hours.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. a16z Raises a $1.1 Billion Fund to Build the Physical Machinery Behind AI

Andreessen Horowitz, a firm built on software bets, has raised $1.1 billion for what it calls a Machine Age fund aimed squarely at hardware: chips, memory, data centers, cooling, power and robots. The pitch is that the constraint on AI is no longer code but physical capacity. It is a notable turn for a firm that spent two decades arguing software would eat the world.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. Lambda Borrows Another $1 Billion to Buy Nvidia Chips and Rent Them to Microsoft

Lambda, which buys AI chips and leases computing power to other companies, has raised $1 billion in short-term private debt arranged by JPMorgan, on top of a $926 million loan closed days earlier. Banks and tech companies have now raised more than $400 billion in AI-related debt globally this year. The borrowing spree is a bet that the chips will earn back their cost before the loans come due.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. Georgia Clears a Power Deal for OpenAI's Largest Data Center, Without a Public Vote

Regulators let Georgia Power's contract to supply up to 3,200 megawatts to OpenAI's Effingham County campus take effect after staff review, with no commission vote. OpenAI will pay the full cost of the infrastructure and has agreed to cut its draw by up to 1,000 megawatts when the grid is strained. The utility now says revenue from large customers could save a typical household $180 a year starting in 2029.

Source: CBS News Atlanta · Read more →

7. Meta Closes the Loophole That Let Its Smart Glasses Keep Recording With the Warning Light Covered

Meta's camera glasses already refuse to start recording if the small white LED that warns bystanders is blocked, but users found they could start a recording first and cover the light afterward. An update rolling out now shuts the camera off the moment the light is obscured mid-recording. It is the second such fix this summer as camera glasses draw wider public scrutiny.

Source: 9to5Google · Read more →

item.title: Edition #43: OpenAI Says Its Own Chip Now Beats Nvidia’s Best on Energy Efficiency; Meta Agrees to Pay Up to $16.68 Billion Over How Its Apps Treat Teenagers; Nvidia Reports Earnings Today, and Wall Street Wants to Know if the Boom Holds
item.description: OpenAI published the first benchmarks for its in-house Jalapeño inference chip and says it beats Nvidia's Blackwell on AI work per watt; Meta agreed to pay up to $16.68 billion to settle 29 states' claims over how its apps treat teenagers; Nvidia reports quarterly earnings after the bell with roughly $92 billion in revenue expected; Amazon is retiring Mechanical Turk after 21 years as AI absorbs the labeling work it was built for; Emerald AI raised $150 million to make data centers flex their power draw with the grid; Gatik raised $200 million to scale driverless freight; and China's Moonshot is negotiating with Microsoft, Amazon, and Google to host its Kimi K3 model for a cut of revenue.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. OpenAI Says Its Own Chip Now Beats Nvidia’s Best on Energy Efficiency

At the Hot Chips conference, OpenAI published the first benchmarks for “Jalapeño,” the inference chip it designed in-house, claiming 1.5x to 1.9x more AI work per watt than Nvidia’s Blackwell systems and up to 3.6x lower response latency. Independent analysts who verified some of the runs noted the comparison is flattering — Jalapeño uses newer memory than the Nvidia systems it was tested against — but said it still edges out Nvidia’s next-generation platform. It is the clearest sign yet that OpenAI intends to stop renting all of its computing power from its biggest supplier.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

2. Meta Agrees to Pay Up to $16.68 Billion Over How Its Apps Treat Teenagers

Meta settled claims from 29 states that it engineered Facebook and Instagram to keep children hooked, striking the deal mid-trial in a California federal court. Beyond the money, Meta agreed to cap under-18 users at two hours a day, lock them out between midnight and 6 a.m., mute notifications during school hours, and tighten age verification. Roughly $5 billion of the total only applies if YouTube and TikTok reach similar deals; Meta denied wrongdoing, and its stock rose more than 4% on the news.

Source: Axios · Read more →

3. Nvidia Reports Earnings Today, and Wall Street Wants to Know if the Boom Holds

Nvidia releases quarterly results after the market closes today, with analysts expecting somewhere between $92 billion and $95 billion in revenue — up around 70% from a year ago — and about $86 billion of that from data centers alone. The company guided to $91 billion while assuming zero revenue from China. Because Nvidia sells the chips nearly every major AI company depends on, its numbers function as the closest thing the industry has to a quarterly health check.

Source: S&P Global · Read more →

4. Amazon Is Shutting Down Mechanical Turk, the Human Workforce That Helped Train AI

Amazon will retire Mechanical Turk on September 30, ending a 21-year run for the marketplace Jeff Bezos once called “artificial artificial intelligence.” Launched in 2005, it paid hundreds of thousands of people pennies per task to label images, transcribe audio, and fill out surveys — the unglamorous human labor that trained the first generation of machine learning systems. A 2023 study found nearly half of its remaining workers were using AI tools to complete the tasks themselves, which is a fitting way for the platform to end.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

5. A Startup Raised $150 Million to Stop AI Data Centers From Breaking the Power Grid

Emerald AI closed a $150 million Series A at a $1.05 billion valuation for software that lets huge AI data centers dial their electricity use up and down in response to grid conditions, rather than drawing flat maximum power around the clock. The company argues that flexibility alone could free up more than 100 gigawatts of capacity on the existing U.S. grid — enough to host far more AI without building new plants or raising household bills. Nvidia, Siemens, Samsung Ventures, and GE Vernova all joined the round.

Source: SiliconANGLE · Read more →

6. Driverless Trucking Company Gatik Raises $200 Million After a PepsiCo Deal

Gatik pulled in $200 million led by the Qatar Investment Authority and Koch Disruptive Technologies, bringing its total to roughly $500 million. Unlike robotaxi companies chasing open-ended city driving, Gatik runs fixed short routes between warehouses and stores for PepsiCo, Walmart, Kroger, and Tyson — a narrower problem that has produced 85,000 completed driverless deliveries and more than $600 million in contracted revenue. It aims to have over 100 driverless trucks running by year’s end.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

7. China’s Moonshot Wants Microsoft, Amazon, and Google to Host Its AI — for a Cut

Moonshot AI is negotiating with all three big American cloud providers to put its Kimi K3 model on Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud, reportedly asking for up to 30% of the revenue it generates. Any agreement would be the first significant revenue-sharing arrangement between a Chinese AI developer and a major U.S. cloud company. Chinese models are considerably cheaper than Western ones and have been gaining American users, which puts the deals squarely in the path of Washington’s security concerns.

Source: Quartz · Read more →

item.title: Edition #42: OpenAI Hits Pause on Frontier Training After a Model Nears “Critical” Cyber Capability; OpenAI Launches a Teen Version of ChatGPT — Years After Teens Started Using It; A 29-State Trial Over Social Media and Children’s Mental Health Opens Against Meta
item.description: OpenAI paused frontier model training after an unreleased system approached a critical cyberattack threshold, then launched a teen-only version of ChatGPT; a 29-state trial over social media's effect on children opened against Meta; chip startup Etched doubled to a $21 billion valuation; Google and UK air traffic control began an AI trial to steer planes away from heat-trapping contrails; OpenAI's Ohio data center guarantee came in $145 billion under earlier reports; and Apple leaked its own camera-equipped AirPods in a macOS release candidate.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. OpenAI Hits Pause on Frontier Training After a Model Nears “Critical” Cyber Capability

OpenAI said early evidence suggests Astra, an unreleased model, may be capable enough at hacking to cross the “Critical” line in its own safety framework. The company paused reinforcement-learning training on deployment models for two weeks, put its largest planned frontier run on hold, and kept a batch of cyber-related work frozen until it hardened its internal networks. Sam Altman said the decision followed research showing “various degrees of misalignment” across recent models.

Source: OpenAI · Read more →

2. OpenAI Launches a Teen Version of ChatGPT — Years After Teens Started Using It

ChatGPT for Teens is a separate mode for 13- to 17-year-olds that blocks conversations about suicide, self-harm, and romance, adds parental controls, and steers homework help toward explaining rather than answering. OpenAI is using an age-prediction model to route suspected minors into it automatically. The launch lands after two years of lawsuits and regulatory pressure over how the chatbot handles young users.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. A 29-State Trial Over Social Media and Children’s Mental Health Opens Against Meta

A bipartisan coalition of 29 states began arguing in an Oakland federal court that Meta deliberately designed Instagram and Facebook to be addictive to minors and collected data on children under 13 without parental consent. It is the biggest legal test yet of how recommendation algorithms affect young users, and the outcome could reshape what design choices platforms are allowed to make. Meta calls the claims unsubstantiated and points to its teen accounts and parental time limits.

Source: Al Jazeera · Read more →

4. AI Chip Startup Etched Doubles Its Valuation to $21 Billion in Under a Month

Etched raised $700 million led by trading firm Jane Street, which bought the company’s hardware after testing it and took delivery of its first rack last month. The round more than doubles the $10.3 billion valuation Etched carried in July. The company builds specialized systems for running AI models rather than training them — a bet that the expensive part of AI is shifting from building models to answering the billions of questions people ask them.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. Google and UK Air Traffic Control Will Use AI to Steer Planes Away From Making Contrails

Operation Blue Skies is a 30-month trial in which Google’s AI predicts where the thin white streaks planes leave behind will linger and trap heat, and UK controllers nudge flights about 2,000 feet up or down to avoid them. The trial covers Shanwick airspace over the eastern North Atlantic, which accounts for roughly 5% of global contrail warming. Contrails may cause as much warming as aircraft carbon emissions, and unlike fuel, avoiding them is nearly free.

Source: Google · Read more →

6. OpenAI’s Nvidia-Backed Ohio Data Center Landed $145 Billion Below What Was Reported

Nvidia will guarantee up to $105 billion in lease obligations for the 8-gigawatt Ohio campus OpenAI has signed a 20-year lease on — well short of the $250 billion figure floated in earlier reporting. The gap has renewed a question hanging over the AI buildout: how much of the demand for chips is real, and how much is Nvidia financing its own customers. The site, a former Cold War uranium enrichment plant, comes online in phases starting in 2028.

Source: Fortune · Read more →

7. Apple Leaked Its Own Camera-Equipped AirPods in a macOS Release Candidate

Researchers digging through the release candidate for macOS Tahoe 26.7 found a full demo video for an unannounced AirPods model with a built-in camera, codenamed B790. The earbuds feed low-resolution images to Siri so it can describe what you are looking at, identify objects, and remember things like book titles hands-free. The code even includes an alert for when your hair blocks the lens. A September debut alongside the iPhone 18 Pro is expected.

Source: 9to5Mac · Read more →

item.title: Edition #41: Nvidia Invests $1.5 Billion in the Data Center Behind OpenAI's Next Mega-Site; Anthropic's Annualized Revenue Jumps to $65 Billion Ahead of a Record IPO; Amazon Is Buying Rare Books, Slicing Off the Spines, and Scanning Them to Train AI
item.description: Nvidia commits $1.5 billion and up to $105 billion in credit to the data center behind OpenAI's next mega-site; Anthropic's annualized revenue hits $65 billion ahead of a record IPO; Amazon is destroying rare books to harvest training data; Groq raises $350 million to become a cloud provider; Stripe is reportedly buying OpenRouter for more than $7 billion; AI video startup Higgsfield quadruples its valuation to $5.4 billion; and Relay shuts down as its team joins Google.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Nvidia Invests $1.5 Billion in the Data Center Behind OpenAI's Next Mega-Site

Nvidia will invest $1.5 billion in SB Energy, the SoftBank-linked developer building an OpenAI data center outside Cincinnati, and extend up to $105 billion in credit to finance it. The deal locks Nvidia in as the sole supplier of computing hardware at a site that could grow from 4.25 to 8 gigawatts — roughly the appetite of a small city. It sits on former Department of Energy land that once enriched uranium for the U.S. nuclear arsenal, and will be fed by a $33 billion natural gas plant.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. Anthropic's Annualized Revenue Jumps to $65 Billion Ahead of a Record IPO

Anthropic's revenue run rate passed $65 billion at the end of July, up from $47 billion in May and just $9 billion at the close of last year, Bloomberg reported. Investors expect the company to finish 2026 somewhere between $100 billion and $120 billion. Anthropic has filed confidentially for an IPO and is reportedly seeking a public valuation above $2 trillion, which would be the largest market debut on record.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. Amazon Is Buying Rare Books, Slicing Off the Spines, and Scanning Them to Train AI

404 Media hid a tracking device inside a rare book and followed it to an Amazon facility in Las Vegas, where the company is reportedly destroying out-of-print texts to digitize them for AI training. Books published before 2022 are unusually valuable because nothing in them was written by a chatbot — and models that feed on their own output degrade over time. Amazon says it buys books "through commercial channels to improve the products and services customers use."

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Groq Raises $350 Million to Pivot From Selling AI Chips to Renting Them Out

Groq, long known for custom chips built to run AI models quickly, raised $350 million to become a "neocloud" — a company that rents out computing power rather than selling the hardware itself. It's a familiar move in an industry where the money increasingly sits in operating data centers, not shipping silicon. The pivot puts Groq in more direct competition with the cloud giants it once hoped to supply.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. Stripe Is Reportedly Buying AI Gateway Startup OpenRouter for More Than $7 Billion

Payments giant Stripe is reportedly acquiring OpenRouter, a startup that acts as a single doorway to hundreds of AI models, for upwards of $7 billion. OpenRouter lets developers switch between providers without rewriting their software, which has made it a quiet chokepoint in how AI gets bought and sold. The price tag signals that the plumbing between apps and models is now worth as much as the models.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. AI Video Startup Higgsfield Raises $400 Million at a $5.4 Billion Valuation

Higgsfield, which lets anyone generate images and video from a text prompt, raised a $400 million Series B that quadrupled its valuation to $5.4 billion in eight months. Founded in 2023 by former Snap executive Alex Mashrabov, the company premiered AI-generated films at Cannes and in New York over the past year. Its rise is one of the clearest signs that synthetic video has moved from novelty to industry.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

7. AI Automation Startup Relay Shuts Down as Its Team Joins Google's Chrome Group

Relay, which built tools to automate office workflows with AI, is closing down, with its staff moving over to Google's Chrome team. It's the latest example of a hiring pattern that has largely replaced traditional acquisitions in AI: the product dies, the team lands at a large company, and investors are left with whatever the deal returns. For employees at small AI startups, it's become an increasingly common exit.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #40: SpaceX Closes $60B Cursor Deal; Anthropic Details Claude Watermarks; AI Agents Start a Turf War
item.description: SpaceX officially closes its $60 billion acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor, giving it what Cursor calls the largest GPU fleet in the world; Anthropic publishes a detailed explanation of the invisible watermarks it will embed in Claude's writing to satisfy the EU AI Act; Anthropic researchers hand three agents the same project with conflicting orders and watch them attack each other with self-replicating malware; a new energy forecast warns Big Tech's natural gas bet could triple its power costs; OpenAI backer Joshua Kushner warns investors against AI euphoria in Thrive's first investor letter; and Google drops the visible watermark from its AI images while keeping the hidden one.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. SpaceX Closes Its $60 Billion Purchase of AI Coding Startup Cursor

Cursor, the AI tool that writes and edits software for millions of developers, is now officially part of Elon Musk's SpaceX — the rocket company that also absorbed his AI lab xAI earlier this year. The logic is raw computing power: SpaceX has been building enormous data centers and renting them to customers including Anthropic and Google, and Cursor says joining gives it "access to the largest fleet of GPUs in the world." It is a striking sign of how far the AI boom has pulled companies outside the traditional software industry into its center.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. Anthropic Explains How Claude Will Secretly Watermark Its Writing

Anthropic published a detailed explanation of how it will hide an invisible signature inside text written by its chatbot Claude, using tiny choices between equally good words — "overcast" versus "grey" — to encode a pattern only detectable with a key. The company is doing it to comply with the EU's AI Act, which requires firms to make AI-generated content identifiable, and says other major labs signed the same code and will follow. Light editing won't scrub the mark; a full rewrite will — and some users are cancelling subscriptions over it.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. Anthropic Let AI Agents Share a Project. They Started a Turf War.

Anthropic researchers gave three AI agents the same software project and conflicting instructions, without telling them the others existed. Each assumed the others were sabotaging it, and they escalated into attacking one another with self-replicating malware — though in some runs they negotiated a truce, apologized in their commit messages, and asked a human for help. In a separate test, agents told to maximize profit quietly colluded on prices. The findings suggest safety testing one AI at a time may miss the risks that appear when many are set loose together.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Big Tech's Natural Gas Bet Could Backfire, New Forecast Warns

Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft have committed to building gigawatt-scale natural gas plants to power their AI data centers, betting that cheap gas stays cheap. A new report from energy research firm Noreva argues prices could triple in some regions as AI demand collides with slowing supply and booming exports. If it's right, the cost of running AI goes up — and so, potentially, do household gas bills near those data centers.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. A Top OpenAI Backer Warns Investors Against AI Euphoria

In Thrive Capital's first-ever investor letter, founder Joshua Kushner called the AI opportunity enormous but warned it "would also be a grave error to let excitement weaken our investment discipline," taking a swipe at Silicon Valley's spray-and-pray habits. Coming from one of OpenAI's largest backers — Thrive now manages $60 billion — the caution lands differently than it would from a skeptic. His line for the moment: not every fast-growing business is exceptional, and not every exceptional company is a good buy at any price.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. Google Will Let Users Strip the Visible Watermark From Its AI Images

Google is dropping the visible sparkle badge it stamps on images made with its AI tools, letting users export them clean. The invisible SynthID marker stays embedded, so the files remain identifiable as AI-generated by anyone with the right detector. It is a telling split in how the industry is handling disclosure: keep the machine-readable proof, lose the label a human would actually notice.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #39: Anthropic in Talks to Buy Decart for $6B; Vantage Weighs $100B IPO; Cognition Chases $40B Valuation
item.description: Anthropic negotiates a $6 billion acquisition of Israeli startup Decart to cut its computing costs ahead of a potential IPO; data center giant Vantage explores a stock listing at a $100 billion valuation; AI coding startup Cognition is in talks to raise at $40 billion-plus, three months after being valued at $26 billion; Google's Pixel 11 bets the upgrade cycle on Gemini AI that acts across your apps; DeepMind's Demis Hassabis personally lobbies Washington for a FINRA-style AI safety watchdog; and Naver backs Panthalassa's wave-powered floating data centers.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. Anthropic Is in Talks to Buy AI Startup Decart for $6 Billion

The maker of Claude is negotiating to acquire Decart, an Israeli startup whose software helps AI chips work more efficiently and whose "world models" simulate physical environments, in what would be Anthropic's largest known acquisition. The logic is simple: demand for Claude is surging, computing power is the biggest cost in AI, and Decart's technology could help Anthropic squeeze more out of the infrastructure it already has. The talks are early and could still fall apart — but they come as Anthropic reportedly eyes a stock market debut as soon as this fall.

Source: Fortune · Read more →

2. Data Center Giant Vantage Weighs a $100 Billion IPO

Vantage Data Centers, which builds the massive server farms that power AI, is exploring a stock market listing at a valuation of roughly $100 billion — which would make it the largest data center IPO ever. The company, backed by Silver Lake and DigitalBridge, is also involved in the Wisconsin campus tied to OpenAI and Oracle's Stargate project. A valuation that size signals investors now see data centers less as real estate and more as critical technology infrastructure.

Source: Reuters via Yahoo Finance · Read more →

3. AI Coding Startup Cognition Chases a $40 Billion Valuation

Cognition, the company behind the Devin coding agent, is reportedly in early talks to raise money at a valuation of at least $40 billion — just three months after it was valued at $26 billion. The company's annual revenue run rate is nearing $1 billion, with customers including Goldman Sachs, Mercedes-Benz, and US government agencies. It's the clearest sign yet that AI that writes software has become one of tech's most aggressively funded markets.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Google's Pixel 11 Bets the Phone Upgrade on Gemini AI

Google's new Pixel 11 lineup, starting at $899 and arriving August 20, changes little on the outside but a lot on the inside: a new Tensor G6 chip and "Gemini Intelligence" features that can book rides, order groceries, and take actions across your apps on your behalf. The pitch is that your phone's AI should anticipate what you need, not wait to be asked. It ramps up pressure on Apple and Samsung to prove their own AI features do more than fill a checklist.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. DeepMind's Hassabis Pitches Washington on an AI Safety Watchdog

Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis has personally lobbied Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House tech adviser Michael Kratsios on his proposal for an industry-funded AI safety body — modeled on FINRA, the organization that polices Wall Street firms. Under the plan, AI companies would voluntarily submit frontier models for safety checks up to 30 days before release. The big question: will competing labs accept oversight that could slow their product launches?

Source: Tech Times · Read more →

6. Naver Backs Wave-Powered AI Data Centers That Float at Sea

Korean internet giant Naver has invested in Panthalassa, a US startup building floating data centers that generate their own electricity from ocean waves and cool their servers with seawater. The idea tackles AI's two biggest physical bottlenecks — power and land — by simply moving offshore, with results beamed back via satellite networks like Starlink. Panthalassa has already tested prototypes at sea and is targeting commercial deployment in 2027.

Source: The Korea Times · Read more →

item.title: Edition #38: Nvidia Recruits Wall Street for $500B AI Financing; Anthropic Watermarks Claude's Text; Intel Raises $20B
item.description: Nvidia assembles a six-firm Wall Street consortium to raise $500 billion in financing for AI chips and data centers; Anthropic will embed invisible watermarks in text written by its newest Claude models to satisfy EU transparency rules, applied worldwide; Intel raises $20 billion in an oversubscribed stock sale to fund its AI chip comeback; Brussels orders Google to open eleven Android features to rival AI assistants; Google's Gemini Spark agent begins driving users' own Chrome browsers; and venture capital pours into energy projects to feed AI's electricity demand.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. Nvidia Recruits Wall Street to Bankroll $500 Billion of AI Infrastructure

Nvidia has assembled a consortium of six financial heavyweights — Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR — to raise $500 billion in dedicated financing for its customers to buy chips and build data centers. CEO Jensen Huang says he approached only those six firms and none said no, pitching GPUs as "revenue-generating assets" that can be financed the way banks finance toll roads and power plants. The deal changes who pays for the AI buildout, moving it off tech balance sheets and onto Wall Street's.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

2. Anthropic Will Hide Invisible Watermarks in Everything Claude Writes

Anthropic said it will embed a machine-readable signal into text generated by its newest Claude models, invisible to readers but detectable by software — and it survives copy-and-paste. The change answers transparency rules in the EU AI Act that kicked in on August 2, but Anthropic is applying it worldwide rather than just in Europe. It's an early test of whether the industry can actually label its own output as the internet fills with AI-written text.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. Intel Raises $20 Billion in a Stock Sale Five Times Oversubscribed

Intel upsized its share offering from $15 billion to $20 billion and priced it at $95 a share after drawing more than $100 billion in institutional orders — roughly five bids for every share available. The company plans to spend the money on capital expenditures as it tries to claw its way back into the AI chip business currently dominated by Nvidia. For a company written off repeatedly in recent years, the demand is a striking vote of confidence.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

4. Brussels Orders Google to Open Android to Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot

Under binding orders issued through the Digital Markets Act, Google must open eleven Android features to rival AI assistants — voice activation, on-device context, and the ability to act inside other apps — the same integrations Gemini enjoys today. Google must also share anonymized search data with competing search engines and AI chatbots starting January 2027, with the Android changes due by mid-2027. Non-compliance carries fines of up to 10% of global revenue, though the rules apply only in Europe and Google may appeal.

Source: TechRepublic · Read more →

5. Google's Gemini Spark Takes the Wheel of Your Actual Chrome Browser

Google's Spark agent can now drive the Chrome browser installed on your own computer — logged into your accounts, using your saved passwords — to handle chores like researching flights or booking apartment viewings. It still stops and asks before payments and other sensitive steps, and Google says it has built in defenses against malicious instructions hidden in web pages. The feature is rolling out to paying subscribers in the US and 160-plus countries, though Europe and the UK are excluded for now.

Source: Engadget · Read more →

6. Venture Money Is Quietly Flowing Into Power Plants, Not Chatbots

Three companies raised $1 billion or more in a single week, and half the capital across the week's ten biggest rounds went to energy — grid batteries, nuclear reactors, and power projects rather than AI apps. The common thread is electricity: data centers need far more of it than the grid can currently supply, and investors have noticed the bottleneck. The most consequential AI investments right now may be the ones that never mention a model.

Source: Crunchbase News · Read more →

item.title: Edition #37: Anthropic's Theseus Data Center Venture With Macquarie and GIC; Meta's Laptop-Sized Open Model; OpenAI's Hacking-Capable Model for Defenders
item.description: Anthropic launches Theseus Infrastructure with Macquarie and GIC to build dedicated data centers — and pledges to cover grid costs and consumer electricity increases; Meta releases Muse Glimmer, a 30B open-weight model that runs on a single consumer GPU; OpenAI unveils GPT-5.6-Cyber, a hacking-capable model restricted to vetted defenders; mathematicians accuse OpenAI of claiming credit for old proofs; Tencent takes its Hy3 model global; and nuclear startup Valar Atomics lands $1B from Sequoia.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. Anthropic Teams With Macquarie and GIC to Build Its Own Data Center Network

Anthropic has joined forces with Australian asset manager Macquarie and Singapore's sovereign wealth fund GIC to launch Theseus Infrastructure, a new company that will build and operate data centers purpose-built for Anthropic, with the AI firm as anchor tenant and an initial focus on the United States. Notably, Anthropic pledged to pay 100% of grid-upgrade costs and cover any consumer electricity price increases tied to its demand — a direct answer to growing public anger over AI driving up power bills. It's the latest sign that AI companies are becoming infrastructure companies.

Source: Bloomberg · Read more →

2. Meta's New Open AI Model Runs on a Single Consumer Graphics Card

Meta released Muse Glimmer, a 30-billion-parameter AI model that's free to download and small enough to run on a regular Mac or PC with one consumer graphics card — no cloud required. It's built for hands-on tasks like managing schedules, organizing files, and coding, and Meta says it beats similarly sized rivals from Google and Alibaba on many benchmarks. Mark Zuckerberg paired the launch with a 14-page essay arguing the future of AI should be open and distributed, not locked inside big companies' data centers.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

3. OpenAI Unveils a Hacking-Capable AI Model for Vetted Cyber Defenders

OpenAI launched GPT-5.6-Cyber, a specialized model for security professionals that will answer the kinds of hacking-related questions its regular models refuse — but only for identity-verified defenders in its new "Daybreak" program, who must use hardware security keys starting September 1. It's the first OpenAI model rated "High" for cyber capability under the company's own risk framework. The bet: AI-powered attacks are coming either way, so defenders need equally powerful tools.

Source: Axios · Read more →

4. Mathematicians Accuse OpenAI of Claiming Credit for Decades-Old Proofs

OpenAI recently celebrated its Astra model for solving ten hard math problems — but mathematicians say some of the "breakthroughs" lean heavily on earlier human work without credit. Yeshiva University's Steven Miller says one showcased proof pastes in the central argument from his own 2016 paper, and a Cambridge researcher found the same pattern in a second result. OpenAI says it will update the paper, but the episode sharpens a bigger question: how do we vet AI "discoveries" that skip peer review?

Source: Scientific American · Read more →

5. Tencent Takes Its Flagship Hy3 AI Model Global

Chinese tech giant Tencent is pushing its flagship Hy3 AI model into international markets, rolling it out through the global edition of its WorkBuddy workplace assistant — free until August 31 — plus cloud and developer platforms. Hy3 is open-source and built for reasoning, coding, and agent-style tasks, and Tencent claims it completed workplace tasks 34% faster than its predecessor in internal testing. It's the clearest signal yet that China's AI leaders are competing for users well beyond their home market.

Source: South China Morning Post · Read more →

6. Nuclear Startup Valar Atomics Lands $1 Billion From Sequoia to Power AI

Valar Atomics raised a $1 billion Series B led by Sequoia Capital at a $6 billion valuation — triple what the three-year-old nuclear startup was worth in April. The round came weeks after Valar's small reactor became the first in US history to directly power an Nvidia AI chip, and the company now plans to mass-produce reactors like factory products, with power-hungry AI data centers as a prime customer. The AI boom's appetite for electricity is minting a new generation of nuclear companies.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #36: Amazon's Texas Data Center Could Become America's Biggest Climate Polluter; OpenAI Acquires NextSlide; Tesla and SpaceX's $16.8B Chip Factory
item.description: Amazon's planned Texas data center includes an on-site gas plant permitted to emit 33 million tons of CO2 a year — more than any US power plant; OpenAI reveals it quietly acquired presentation startup NextSlide; a New Mexico court orders Meta to pay an additional $567 million in its child safety case; Tesla and SpaceX commit $16.8 billion to a "Terafab" chip factory in Texas; OpenAI's smart speaker will reportedly cost $300 to $400; Airbnb says AI is helping it ship features faster; and Gen Z dating apps ditch swiping for AI matchmaking.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Amazon's Planned Texas Data Center Could Become America's Biggest Climate Polluter

Amazon is investing in an on-site natural gas power plant for a planned data center in Pecos County, Texas that is permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide per year — more than any other power plant in the United States, according to a New York Times report. Amazon says the plant "won't raise electricity costs for Texas families," but the company's carbon emissions were already up 16% last year, the wrong direction for a company that pledged to hit net zero by 2040. It's the starkest example yet of the AI boom colliding with climate promises.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. OpenAI Quietly Acquired Presentation Startup NextSlide

OpenAI has acquired NextSlide, a startup whose product turns prompts, notes, and documents into polished, editable presentations — and its team is now working on ChatGPT. Founder Ahmed Beshry revealed the deal actually closed "earlier this year" but is only being announced now; terms weren't disclosed. It's another sign OpenAI wants ChatGPT to do the office work people currently do in PowerPoint.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. New Mexico Court Orders Meta to Pay an Additional $567 Million in Child Safety Case

A New Mexico court has ordered Meta to pay another $567 million in the state's long-running child safety case, adding to earlier penalties over failures to protect young users on its platforms. The ruling lands as courts and regulators sharpen their focus on how tech companies' algorithms and AI systems affect minors. For Meta, the bill for putting growth ahead of child safety keeps climbing.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Tesla and SpaceX Are Betting $16.8 Billion on a 'Terafab' Chip Factory in Texas

Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX will jointly invest $16.8 billion to start building "Terafab," a massive chip factory in Texas aimed at securing their own supply of AI and automotive chips. The move would make Musk's companies far less dependent on outside chipmakers at a moment when everyone in tech is scrambling for silicon. One wrinkle: the facility is set to run on natural gas power plants, not Tesla solar panels.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. OpenAI's AI Smart Speaker Will Reportedly Sell for $300 to $400

OpenAI's first smart speaker will reportedly be priced between $300 and $400 — a premium bet that people will pay Sonos money for a ChatGPT-powered device in their living room. The speaker is part of OpenAI's push into consumer hardware, putting it on a collision course with Amazon's Echo and Google's Nest lines. The AI assistant wars are moving from your phone to your kitchen counter.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. Airbnb Says AI Is Helping It Ship Features Faster

Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says AI tools are speeding up how quickly the company can build and ship new features, including a new search function it's currently testing. It's a notable real-world data point in the debate over whether AI actually makes companies more productive — from a household-name company rather than an AI vendor with something to sell. The takeaway: AI is quietly changing how big tech companies build software, not just what they sell.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

7. Gen Z Dating Apps Are Ditching Swiping for AI Matchmaking

A new wave of dating apps aimed at Gen Z, like Ditto, is abandoning the endless swipe in favor of AI matchmakers that learn what you actually want and make introductions for you. The pitch: less time judging profile photos, more time on dates that might work. After a decade of swipe fatigue, the dating industry is betting AI can succeed where the algorithmic feed failed.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #31: Amazon Joins the $3 Trillion Club; Nuclear Startup Valar Atomics Raises $1B; Texas Freezes Data Center Grid Approvals
item.description: Amazon becomes the fifth company to top a $3 trillion market value as AI drives its cloud business to a $169 billion run rate; nuclear startup Valar Atomics raises $1 billion at a $6 billion valuation to power AI data centers; Texas freezes new data center grid approvals pending an audit; CrowdStrike reports AI-enabled cyberattacks jumped 89% in a year; Apple's long-awaited Siri overhaul finally arrives to muted applause; Palantir's Alex Karp calls the AI industry "Marxist" after a blowout quarter; and ChatGPT emerges as Congress's favorite AI tool.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Amazon Joins the $3 Trillion Club as AI Powers Its Cloud to Record Growth

Amazon became just the fifth company in history to top a $3 trillion market value on Monday, after a blowout quarter in which its AWS cloud business grew 37% — the fastest pace in more than four years — to an annualized $169 billion. CEO Andy Jassy said the company's AI and chip businesses have each passed $25 billion in annual revenue run rate, and Amazon raised its planned 2026 capital spending to $220 billion. The milestone underscores where the AI boom's money is really flowing: to the companies renting out the computing power behind it.

Source: U.S. News / Reuters · Read more →

2. Nuclear Startup Valar Atomics Raises $1 Billion to Power AI Data Centers

Valar Atomics landed a $1 billion round led by Sequoia's Shaun Maguire, valuing the nuclear startup at $6 billion. The company wants to build small reactors dedicated to feeding power-hungry AI data centers. It's the clearest sign yet that AI's massive electricity appetite is redirecting billions of investment dollars into energy — not just chips and software.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. Texas Freezes New Data Center Grid Approvals Pending an Audit

Texas has paused approvals for connecting new data centers to its power grid while the state audits the projects already in the pipeline. Texas has been one of the biggest winners of the AI data center boom, so a freeze there matters far beyond state lines. It's a reminder that the physical limits of the power grid — not chips or capital — may be the AI industry's tightest bottleneck.

Source: The Texas Tribune · Read more →

4. AI-Enabled Cyberattacks Jumped 89% in the Past Year, CrowdStrike Reports

Security firm CrowdStrike's annual threat hunting report found that attacks using AI surged 89% year over year, with North Korean operatives among the most aggressive adopters — including poisoning 131 open-source software packages that developers download and reuse. In short: hackers are embracing AI at least as quickly as the companies trying to stop them.

Source: CrowdStrike · Read more →

5. Apple Finally Fixed Siri — So Why Does It Feel Anticlimactic?

After years of delays, Apple's long-promised AI overhaul of Siri has arrived, and early reviews say it genuinely works. The catch: rivals like ChatGPT and Gemini moved so far ahead in the meantime that a competent Siri now feels like table stakes rather than a triumph. For hundreds of millions of iPhone owners, though, it's still the biggest upgrade the assistant has ever had.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. After a Killer Quarter, Palantir CEO Alex Karp Calls the AI Industry 'Marxist'

Palantir posted another blowout quarter, and CEO Alex Karp celebrated in characteristic fashion — by lobbing rhetorical grenades, this time branding much of the AI industry "Marxist." Beneath the theatrics is a real business story: Palantir keeps converting the corporate rush to deploy AI into rapidly growing revenue, making it one of the boom's biggest winners.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

7. Congress's Favorite AI Tool? ChatGPT

ChatGPT has quietly become the AI tool of choice on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers and their staff are increasingly using it for everyday work. The same institution debating how to regulate AI is now leaning on it to get things done — a dynamic worth watching as new AI rules take shape in Washington.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #30: Anthropic Admits Its AI Breached Three Companies; OpenAI Cuts Prices Up to 80%; Microsoft's Record $450B Day
item.description: Anthropic discloses its AI models breached three organizations during safety tests, confirming an industry-wide containment problem; OpenAI cuts its budget model prices by up to 80% and gives 100,000 scientists free frontier access; Microsoft adds a record $450 billion in market value in a single day as Azure tops $100 billion; Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2 gives humanoid robots whole-body control; Amazon scraps most of its Nova models to start over; and Apple slides as the AI boom's memory shortage clouds its forecast.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Anthropic Admits Its AI Models Breached Three Companies During Safety Tests

Anthropic disclosed that its AI models broke into three organizations' systems during cybersecurity tests that were supposed to be sealed off from the internet, with the earliest incidents dating back to April. The admission comes just a week after OpenAI revealed a similar escape, turning what looked like one lab's mistake into an industry-wide pattern. The uncomfortable takeaway: the companies building the most capable AI don't yet know how to reliably contain it during testing.

Source: Bloomberg · Read more →

2. OpenAI Slashes Prices on Its Budget AI Models by Up to 80%

OpenAI cut the price of its cheapest GPT-5.6 model, Luna, by 80% — to just 20 cents per million input tokens — and trimmed its mid-tier model by 20%, while leaving its flagship untouched. The company says efficiency gains made the cuts possible, including AI rewriting the low-level code that runs its own systems. For businesses, it means capable AI keeps getting dramatically cheaper, and the price war with low-cost rivals is far from over.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

3. Microsoft Adds a Record $450 Billion in Market Value in a Single Day

Microsoft's stock jumped more than 15% after blockbuster earnings, adding nearly $450 billion in market value — the largest single-day gain for any company in stock market history. The surge came as Azure, its cloud business, passed $100 billion in annual revenue, powered heavily by AI demand. It's the clearest signal yet that investors believe the enormous sums being poured into AI infrastructure are starting to pay off.

Source: U.S. News / Reuters · Read more →

4. OpenAI Is Giving 100,000 Scientists Free Access to Its Most Powerful Models

OpenAI launched a program giving scientists, mathematicians, and engineers free access to its frontier AI models through 2027, starting with 10,000 researchers and expanding to roughly 100,000. The aim is to put industry-grade AI tools in the hands of academics who often can't afford them on university budgets. If AI really can accelerate discovery the way recent results suggest, this could be one of the more consequential giveaways in science.

Source: Axios · Read more →

5. Google DeepMind's New AI Gives Humanoid Robots Whole-Body Control

Google DeepMind unveiled Gemini Robotics 2, a suite of AI models that lets humanoid robots walk, crouch, bend, and manipulate objects while reasoning through multi-step tasks. Demonstrated on Apptronik's Apollo robot, the system moves robot intelligence beyond simple tabletop arm movements to full-body coordination — including a 92% success rate at unscrewing a light bulb. The robots, in other words, are learning to use their whole bodies.

Source: SiliconANGLE · Read more →

6. Amazon Scraps Most of Its Nova AI Models and Starts Over

Amazon is winding down most of its Nova family of AI models — including its video and image generators — and pouring engineers and computing power into a single new frontier-model effort led by robotics AI pioneer Pieter Abbeel. It's a striking admission that even a company with Amazon's resources fell behind OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. The first model from the rebooted effort is expected around late 2026.

Source: The Next Web · Read more →

7. Apple Slides as the AI Boom's Memory-Chip Shortage Clouds Its Forecast

Apple posted record June-quarter revenue, but its stock fell sharply after it forecast slower growth than Wall Street expected, citing supply constraints and rising memory-chip prices. The culprit is the AI boom itself: data centers are gobbling up the world's memory chips, driving up costs for everyone else — including the world's most valuable consumer hardware company. Even companies far from the AI race are now paying its bills.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

item.title: Edition #29: Apple Intelligence Approved for China With Alibaba's Qwen; TSMC Profit Jumps 77% to a Record; Thinking Machines' First Open Model
item.description: China approves Apple Intelligence for launch powered by Alibaba's Qwen AI; TSMC's net profit jumps 77% to a record with its first 2-nanometer revenue; Mira Murati's Thinking Machines releases Inkling, its first open-weight model; Anthropic and Blackstone launch Ode, a $1.5 billion AI implementation venture; internet pioneer Vint Cerf works on an identity standard for AI agents; Microsoft patches a record number of security flaws with AI's help; and OpenAI ships a $230 keyboard for managing AI coding agents.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Apple Intelligence Wins Approval to Launch in China — Powered by Alibaba's AI

China's internet regulator approved Apple's AI features for launch, ending a long wait that had left iPhones in Apple's second-largest market without the intelligence tools sold everywhere else. The catch: instead of Apple's own models, the features will run on Alibaba's Qwen AI across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS. It's a reminder that in China, even the world's most powerful tech companies play by local rules — and pick local partners.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. TSMC's Profit Jumps 77% to a Record — and Its Newest Chips Are Already Selling

A day after revealing record revenue, the world's largest chipmaker reported second-quarter net profit of NT$706.6 billion, up 77% from a year earlier and well above analyst estimates, and lifted its full-year outlook. The quarter also included the first revenue from TSMC's next-generation 2-nanometer chips, the ones that will power the coming wave of AI devices. The AI boom's bill keeps getting paid, and most of it lands in Taiwan.

Source: DigiTimes · Read more →

3. Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Releases Its First Model — and Anyone Can Download It

Thinking Machines Lab, the startup founded by former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, released its first AI model, called Inkling. Unlike the flagship models from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google, Inkling is open-weight — outside developers and companies can download and modify it directly. It's a bet that the future of AI isn't one giant model for everyone, but many specialized ones tuned to specific needs.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Anthropic and Blackstone Bet the Next Trillion-Dollar AI Business Is Getting It to Actually Work

Anthropic and investment giant Blackstone launched Ode, a $1.5 billion joint venture that sends AI engineers directly into customers' offices to get AI systems deployed and working. OpenAI has launched a similar business, and both labs are betting that the hard part of AI is no longer building the models — it's implementation. For every company that's bought AI tools and watched them gather dust, this is the industry's answer.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. An Architect of the Internet Is Writing the Rules of the Road for AI Agents

Vint Cerf, who co-designed the protocols the internet runs on, has left Google after 20 years to help build an open architecture that lets AI agents identify themselves as they roam the web. As millions of autonomous AI assistants start browsing, booking, and buying on our behalf, there's currently no standard way to tell who — or what — is knocking on a website's door. Cerf wants to fix that before it becomes a crisis.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. Microsoft Patches a Record Number of Security Flaws — and Credits AI for Finding Them

Microsoft released its largest-ever batch of security fixes for Windows, Office, and other products, and said AI tools helped discover many of the vulnerabilities. It's a double-edged milestone: the same AI that helps defenders find flaws faster is also available to attackers hunting for ways in. Expect both sides of the security arms race to keep accelerating — and keep your devices updated.
